how_it_realizes_D: Python's own package/import system IS the typed dependency graph: core/ (no project imports allowed out), domains/<name>/ (may import core.* only), app/ (the sole broad-import composition root). Edges are literal `import` statements resolvable via ast, so the graph is not a diagram but the real, checkable source structure. domains.tasks.service.assign() deliberately does NOT verify the assignee exists in domains.users -- that cross-domain check lives only in app/main.py::assign_task, demonstrating the composition-root-only rule concretely (a real "should-use-but-does-not" case, not just a lint rule with nothing to bite).
boundary_enforcer: Two enforcers for the same rules: (1) .importlinter -- declarative import-linter contracts (layers: app>domains>core; independence: domains.users vs domains.tasks), not runnable offline since import-linter isn't installed in this sandbox (verified: `python3 -c "import importlinter"` -> ModuleNotFoundError), but written and wired into `make boundary-lint` to run automatically if present. (2) tools/boundary_check.py -- a zero-dependency stdlib script (ast-based) that is the actual enforced gate: fails on any domains.X -> domains.Y import (Y != X), any domain -> app import, any core -> domains/app import, AND on any file outside core/ids.py defining to_base62/from_base62/new_id/validate_title/validate_email or any function with 'base62' in its name. Verified live: injected a fake `from domains.tasks.service import TaskStore` into domains/users/service.py (caught, exit 1), injected a duplicate `def to_base62` into domains/tasks/service.py (caught, exit 1), both reverted afterward. In the process of testing this I found and fixed a real bug in the shared import-resolution helper (tools/_pygraph.py) where absolute imports were incorrectly being prefixed with the importing file's own package, which silently made the enforcer blind to real violations until fixed.
manifest_generation: tools/gen_manifest.py walks core/, domains/*, app/ with Python's ast module (via the shared tools/_pygraph.py helper also used by boundary_check.py), collecting every public top-level function/class as a capability mapped to its owning file, and every resolvable project-local import as a dependency edge. `make manifest` (gen_manifest.py) regenerates manifest.json; `make manifest-check` (gen_manifest.py --check) regenerates in memory, diffs against the committed manifest.json, and fails (with a unified diff) on any mismatch -- verified live by adding an undeclared function to core/ids.py (check correctly failed and printed the diff) then reverting (check passed again). This is the CI drift-check gate, run as the last step of `make ci` and of .github/workflows/ci.yml.

language: TypeScript / Node (Node >=22, tsc >=5.7 — verified locally with Node v25.9.0 and tsc 6.0.2)
how_it_realizes_D: TypeScript project references (tsconfig `references` arrays) are the typed build DAG: each package's tsconfig.json declares exactly which other packages it may import types/files from (core: none; users: [core]; tasks: [core]; app: [core, users, tasks]). `tsc -b` (composite builds, `allowImportingTsExtensions` + `emitDeclarationOnly` so the same .ts sources both type-check and run natively via `node file.ts`, no separate JS build to keep in sync) walks this graph and structurally cannot resolve a file belonging to a project that isn't referenced — verified live: adding `import { listTasks } from '../../tasks/src/index.ts'` into packages/users/src/index.ts with no matching `references` entry makes `tsc -b .` fail with TS6059/TS6307 (file not under rootDir / not listed in project file list), proving the edges are load-bearing, not decorative.
boundary_enforcer: Two enforcers checking the same two rules (no domain-to-domain import; no duplicate/base62-lookalike primitive outside core): (1) `.dependency-cruiser.js` — real forbidden-rule config (no-users-importing-tasks, no-tasks-importing-users, core-must-not-depend-on-domains-or-app, no-duplicate-base62-outside-core), the idiomatic tool, requires `npm install` so untested offline here; (2) `tools/boundary-lint.mjs` — Node-stdlib-only (fs/path, no node_modules) script sharing `tools/lib/scan.mjs`'s regex-based import/declaration parser, wired as `npm run lint:boundaries` and into CI; verified live to fail (exit 1) on an injected users→tasks import and on an injected duplicate `encodeBase62*` function outside core, and to pass clean (exit 0) on the real tree.
manifest_generation: `tools/gen-manifest.mjs` (Node stdlib only, reuses tools/lib/scan.mjs) walks packages/*/src and packages/*/test, extracting every exported top-level declaration into a capability→owning-file map and every relative import into package-level and file-level dependency edges, then serializes deterministically (sorted, no timestamps) to manifest.json via `--write`. `--check` regenerates in memory and byte-diffs against the committed file, exiting 1 on mismatch — wired as `npm run check:manifest`, the last step of `npm run ci` and of .github/workflows/ci.yml. Verified live: `--write`/`--check` round-trip clean; injecting a new exported function without regenerating makes `--check` fail with an explicit drift message, and regenerating fixes it.

language: TypeScript (Next.js App Router layout), with plain-Node ESM (.mjs) stdlib tooling
how_it_realizes_D: Design D's typed dependency graph is realized directly by Next.js/Node's own module system plus a path-prefix domain classifier: src/core (no internal deps), src/features/users and src/features/tasks (each depends on core only, never on each other — tasks/service.ts assigns tasks via a bare `assigneeId: string`, never importing the User type), src/composition/root.ts (the one file importing both features), and src/app (imports composition only, never features directly). The edges aren't just convention — scripts/lib/graph.mjs parses every real `import`/`export...from` statement in src/ into a file-and-domain-level graph, which both the boundary enforcer and the manifest generator consume, so 'typed edges' means a graph mechanically derived from actual imports, checked against one shared allow-list table (ALLOWED_EDGES in scripts/lib/rules.mjs, mirrored in eslint.config.mjs's boundaries/element-types rule).
boundary_enforcer: Two enforcers checking the identical edge table: (1) eslint.config.mjs using eslint-plugin-boundaries (idiomatic tool, not installed/run in this offline scaffold but wired into CI which installs it), and (2) scripts/check-boundaries.mjs — a zero-dependency stdlib Node script (scripts/lib/graph.mjs + scripts/lib/rules.mjs) that parses imports via regex, resolves them to files/domains, and fails (exit 1) on: (a) any domain-to-domain edge outside the allow-list (in particular users<->tasks), (b) code outside src/core that looks like a base62 encoder or duplicates validateEmail/validateTitle, (c) a 'use client' file importing the server-only composition root, (d) a duplicated `// @capability` marker. scripts/check-boundaries.test.mjs proves it actually fires, via 7 synthetic-fixture tests (all passing) covering every violation type plus the clean-graph pass case; I also live-tested it against the real tree by temporarily adding `import { getUser } from "../users"` to tasks/service.ts and confirmed check-boundaries.mjs failed with the exact expected message, then reverted.
manifest_generation: scripts/generate-manifest.mjs calls the same loadSourceGraph() used by the boundary checker (scripts/lib/graph.mjs), extracts `// @capability <id>` markers (capability -> owning file), rolls up parsed imports into file-level and domain-level edge sets, and serializes deterministically (sorted keys/arrays, no timestamps) to MANIFEST.generated.json — never hand-authored. `--check` mode regenerates in memory and byte-compares against the committed file, exiting 1 with a fix-it message on drift; this is wired as the third step of node scripts/ci.mjs / make ci / .github/workflows/ci.yml. Live-verified: adding a new file to src/core/ made --check fail with 'MANIFEST.generated.json is stale'; regenerating and removing the file restored a clean pass.
how_to_run: cd starters/nextjs && node scripts/ci.mjs   (equivalently: npm run ci, or make ci). This runs, fully offline with only the global `tsc` binary + Node stdlib: (1) tsc -p tsconfig.build.json to compile src/**/*.{ts,tsx} to dist/ as CommonJS, using ambient shims in src/types/*.d.ts standing in for @types/react and @types/node since no npm install was run; (2) node --test 'dist/**/*.test.js' 'scripts/**/*.test.mjs' — 15 tests, all passing (4 users, 4 tasks, 7 boundary-enforcer self-tests); (3) node scripts/check-boundaries.mjs — 21 files scanned, 0 violations; (4) node scripts/generate-manifest.mjs --check — up to date. You can also run `node dist/composition/run.js` after building to see the wired user+tasks scenario execute end to end. `npm run dev/build/start` (real Next.js) are declared but intentionally not run/installed per the no-network-installs constraint; see README.md's 'What is not run offline' section.

language: Rust (Cargo workspace, edition 2021, stable toolchain, zero crates.io dependencies)
how_it_realizes_D: Cargo's native workspace + [dependencies] system IS the typed dependency graph: each crate's Cargo.toml [dependencies] table is a compiler-enforced edge (rustc refuses `use` of any crate not listed there). crates/core (package name `corelib`, to avoid colliding with Rust's sysroot `core`) has zero workspace deps and holds base62 encode/decode (base62.rs) and validate_title/validate_email (validate.rs) as the sole homes for those primitives. crates/users and crates/tasks each declare exactly one workspace dependency, `corelib = { path = "../core" }` -- no users<->tasks edge exists to remove because tasks references its assignee only as an opaque `assignee_id: Option<String>`, never as `users::User`. crates/app is the composition root and the only crate whose Cargo.toml legitimately lists more than one domain (corelib, users, tasks), wiring both stores together in a tiny end-to-end scenario (create user, create/assign/list tasks, look up by id).
boundary_enforcer: xtask (a zero-dependency stdlib-only binary at xtask/src/main.rs, run via `cargo run -p xtask -- boundary-lint`). It reads every crate's Cargo.toml with a small hand-rolled TOML-section reader (no `toml` crate) and asserts: (a) no domain's workspace deps contain another domain's package name, (b) each domain's workspace deps equal exactly {corelib} (no more, no less), (c) core has zero workspace deps, and (d) greps every crates/*/src/**/*.rs file OUTSIDE crates/core for base62-shaped markers (base62, %62, ALPHABET, 62usize/62u64) and fails listing file+line if any are found -- the grep-based duplicate-primitive rule. I proved this is a real, non-decorative check by temporarily adding `tasks = { path = \"../tasks\" }` to crates/users/Cargo.toml plus a fake `% 62` line in users/src/lib.rs, re-ran boundary-lint, watched it report all 3 violations with exit failure, then reverted and reconfirmed a clean pass. xtask also has its own #[test]s asserting boundary_lint(&workspace_root()) == Ok(()), so `cargo test` catches regressions too, not just the standalone lint command.
manifest_generation: `xtask manifest-gen` (same zero-dep binary) walks every crate's src/ tree for `/// capability: <name>` doc-comment markers, records the file+line of the next real item each one documents, and separately re-parses every Cargo.toml (same reader boundary-lint uses) for the live dependency edges; it renders both into MANIFEST.md as two tables (capability -> owning file; dependency edges), fully derived, never hand-typed. `xtask manifest-check` regenerates the same content in memory and byte-compares it against the committed MANIFEST.md, failing (exit 1) if they differ -- this is the CI drift check, also covered by its own #[test] in xtask so plain `cargo test` catches manifest staleness too.
how_to_run: cd starters/rust && cargo build --workspace --offline && cargo test --workspace --offline && cargo run -p xtask --offline -- boundary-lint && cargo run -p xtask --offline -- manifest-check && cargo run -p app --offline   (equivalently: `just ci` runs build+test+boundary-lint+manifest-check as one target; .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the same four steps on push/PR). All verified locally with cargo 1.93.1 / rustc 1.93.1: build succeeded, 15/15 tests passed across corelib(6)/tasks(3)/users(4)/xtask(2), boundary-lint passed, manifest-check passed with zero drift, and the app binary produced the expected scenario output.

language: Java (JDK 21+, plain javac/java, JPMS modules — no build tool)
how_it_realizes_D: The dependency graph is JPMS's own module-info.java requires/exports, compiled by plain javac (no build tool). taskly.core exports taskly.core.id (Base62Encoder) and taskly.core.validate (Validators) — the ONE home for each primitive. taskly.users and taskly.tasks each `requires taskly.core` only; neither requires the other, and Task.assigneeId is a plain String (no type-level reference to User), so a users<->tasks edge is structurally impossible, not just undeclared. taskly.app is the sole module allowed to require all three (composition root) and Main.java is the only file importing both domains, wiring them at the value level. Verified live: temporarily adding `import taskly.users.User;` to TaskService.java with no matching `requires` produced a real javac error ("package taskly.users is not visible ... module taskly.tasks does not read it"); temporarily adding `requires taskly.users;` to tasks/module-info.java (a legal-but-wrong module graph javac would accept) was caught instead by BoundaryCheck.
boundary_enforcer: Two layers, both exercised and confirmed working: (1) the javac/JPMS compiler itself — a domain module-info.java that omits `requires <other-domain>` makes any import from that domain a compile error, reproduced above; (2) tools/src/tools/BoundaryCheck.java, a ~150-line dependency-free plain-Java tool (chosen over ArchUnit, which needs a network dependency fetch unavailable here) that (a) parses each domain module-info.java and fails if it requires another domain module, and (b) scans every non-core .java file (comments stripped first, to avoid false positives from javadoc examples) for a redefined requireEmail/requireNonEmpty, a class named like a base62 encoder, the literal base62 alphabet string, or %62/ /62 arithmetic — concrete tells of a duplicated primitive. Run via tools/boundary-check.sh or `make boundary-lint`.
manifest_generation: tools/src/tools/ManifestGen.java parses every module's module-info.java (comments stripped) for requires/exports to build the modules+edges sections, and walks each module's src/main/java tree to find the first public top-level type per file, slugifying PascalCase to kebab-case to name each capability (e.g. Base62Encoder -> base62-encoder) with its owning file path and module. Output is deterministic (no timestamps, sorted) so two runs against unchanged source are byte-identical. tools/generate-manifest.sh writes manifest.json; `tools/generate-manifest.sh --check` (run as CI's last step) regenerates into a temp file and diffs it against the committed manifest.json, failing the build with the diff shown if it's stale — the drift check.

boundary_enforcer: tools/boundary_lint.sh (bash 3.2-compatible, sourcing tools/lib_graph.sh) — parses every src/*.pas file's unit/program name and single-line `uses` clause with grep/sed, classifies files as core (src/core.pas) / root (the `program`, app.pas) / domain (everything else under src/) by structural convention (not a hardcoded domain-name list, so it generalizes to future domains), then (a) fails if any domain file's `uses` clause names another file classified domain, and (b) reads core.pas's own interface-section function/procedure names and fails if any non-core src/*.pas file defines a top-level function/procedure with the same name. Verified live: clean tree passes; injecting `uses Tasks;` into users.pas and separately injecting a duplicate `function Base62Encode` into users.pas each made the script exit 1 with a specific error naming the file and rule violated, then the file was restored and the tree re-verified clean.
how_it_realizes_D: Free Pascal's `unit`/`program` declaration plus its `uses` clause is not documentation of a dependency, it's the actual mechanism fpc uses to resolve symbols and link the binary — so the typed dependency graph Design D asks for already exists natively in the source, with zero extra ceremony. core.pas exports Base62Encode/IsNonEmptyTitle/IsValidEmail from its interface and has no uses clause naming any domain (in-degree 0 within the app graph). users.pas and tasks.pas each declare exactly one edge, `uses Core;`, in their implementation section, and have no way to reference each other's types because neither names the other in a uses clause — the compiler itself would refuse Users.SomeCall(Tasks.Thing) without that declaration. app.pas is the sole file with `uses SysUtils, Core, Users, Tasks;`, wiring both domains together by passing a Users-minted id string into Tasks.AssignTask (Tasks stores it as an opaque string field, never importing TUser). The "should-use-but-does-not" rule (no domain-to-domain edge) is a negative constraint fpc alone won't enforce (it would happily compile Users importing Tasks), so tools/boundary_lint.sh supplies that check by reading the same uses clauses back out of the source text.
manifest_generation: manifest.json is produced by tools/gen_manifest.sh, which sources tools/lib_graph.sh and (1) extracts every function/procedure name declared in core.pas's interface section as the "capabilities" map, (2) extracts every unit/program name under src/ plus its core/root/domain classification as "modules", and (3) extracts every (from-unit, to-unit, file) triple from each file's uses clause as "edges" — nothing hand-typed. tools/check_manifest_drift.sh regenerates into a temp file and diffs it against the committed manifest.json, failing CI with a unified diff if they differ (verified live: a corrupted manifest.json was replaced with `{"stale": true}` and the drift check correctly exited 1 with the diff shown; regeneration was also shown to be idempotent — re-running gen_manifest.sh against the unchanged source produces byte-identical output).
